question: The lecture proved that for a continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) the sequence of Riemann sums \(S(f,X_n)\) converges as the norm \(\|X_n\|\) of the partitions tends to zero.  Using the definition of the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f(\eta)\), explain why the continuity of \(f\) guarantees that the limit of these Riemann sums is independent of the chosen sequence of partitions and equals the integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
answer:
Because \(f\) is continuous on the compact interval \([a,b]\), its modulus of continuity satisfies \(\omega_f(\eta)\to 0\) as \(\eta\to 0\).  For any two partitions \(X\) and \(Y\) with norms less than \(\delta\), the inequality from the first question gives
\[
|S(f,X)-S(f,Y)|\le\omega_f(\delta)(b-a).
\]
Letting \(\delta\to0\) forces the difference between any two Riemann sums with sufficiently fine partitions to become arbitrarily small, so the sequence \(S(f,X_n)\) is Cauchy and converges to a unique limit.  This limit is independent of the chosen sequence of partitions and is defined to be the integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).

question: According to the discussion, Riemann sums are linear in the function being integrated.  Show how this linearity property leads to the linearity of the integral for continuous functions \(f\) and \(g\) and a scalar \(\alpha\), i.e. prove that \(\int_a^b (\alpha f + g)(x)\,dx = \alpha\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b g(x)\,dx\).  Explain the role of continuity in this argument.
answer:
For any tagged partitions \(X\) and any functions \(f,g\) and scalar \(\alpha\), the Riemann sum satisfies
\[
S(\alpha f+g,X)=\alpha S(f,X)+S(g,X).
\]
Taking limits as the norm of \(X\) tends to zero and using the existence of the integrals for continuous \(f\) and \(g\) gives
\[
\int_a^b (\alpha f+g)(x)\,dx = \alpha\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b g(x)\,dx.
\]

answer: Because \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\), it is uniformly continuous. Hence for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\) whenever \(|x-y|<\delta\). If two partitions have mesh size smaller than \(\delta\), the oscillation of \(f\) on each subinterval is less than \(\varepsilon/(b-a)\). The difference between any two Riemann sums is then bounded by \((b-a)\cdot\varepsilon/(b-a)=\varepsilon\). Thus the sums can be made arbitrarily close, and they all converge to the same limit.

question: According to the lecture, theorem 2 allows comparison of two Riemann sums when one partition is finer than the other. Using this theorem, show how the Riemann sum of a continuous function \(f\) over a coarse partition can be bounded by the Riemann sums over a finer partition that refines it.
answer: Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a coarse partition and \(\mathcal{Q}\) a finer partition such that \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{Q}\). For each subinterval \(I\) of \(\mathcal{P}\), the subintervals of \(\mathcal{Q}\) that lie inside \(I\) form a refinement of \(I\). By theorem 2, the Riemann sum over \(\mathcal{P}\) lies between the Riemann sums over the two extreme refinements of \(\mathcal{P}\) obtained by taking the infimum and supremum of \(f\) on each \(I\). Since \(f\) is continuous, the infimum and supremum on each \(I\) are close when the mesh of \(\mathcal{Q}\) is small, so the coarse sum is squeezed between two fine sums that are themselves close. Hence the coarse Riemann sum is bounded by the fine Riemann sums.

question: Consider two tagged partitions \(P\) and \(P'\) of \([a,b]\) whose norms satisfy \(\|P\|<\delta\) and \(\|P'\|<\delta\). Using the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f\) of a continuous function \(f\) and the triangle inequality, explain why the difference \(|S(f,P)-S(f,P')|\) can be made arbitrarily small as \(\delta\to0\).
answer:
By Theorem 3 we have\\[
    |S(f,P)-S(f,P')|\le\bigl(\omega_f(\|P\|)+\omega_f(\|P'\|)\bigr)(b-a).
    \\]Since \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\), choose \(\delta>0\) so that \(\omega_f(\delta)<\varepsilon/(2(b-a))\). Then for any \(P,P'\) with norms \(<\delta\) the right‑hand side is \(<\varepsilon\), proving the difference can be made arbitrarily small.

question: Let \((P_n)\) be a sequence of tagged partitions of \([a,b]\) with \(\|P_n\|\to0\). Show that the corresponding sequence of Riemann sums \((S(f,P_n))\) is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, and explain why it converges to a real number \(I\).
answer:
Using the same estimate as above, for any \(m,n\)\\[
    |S(f,P_m)-S(f,P_n)|\le\bigl(\omega_f(\|P_m\|)+\omega_f(\|P_n\|)\bigr)(b-a).
    \\]Because \(\|P_n\|\to0\), given \(\varepsilon>0\) choose \(N\) so that for \(k\ge N\) we have \(\|P_k\|<\delta\) with \(\omega_f(\delta)<\varepsilon/(2(b-a))\). Then for \(m,n\ge N\) the difference is \(<\varepsilon\). Thus \((S(f,P_n))\) is Cauchy. The real numbers are complete, so the sequence converges to some real number \(I\).

question: Suppose \(I\) is defined as the limit of Riemann sums for a particular sequence of partitions \((P_n)\) with \(\|P_n\|\to0\). Write\\[
    |S(f,Q_n)-I|\le |S(f,Q_n)-S(f,P_n)|+|S(f,P_n)-I|.

Thus for any \(\eta<\delta\) all elements of the set \(\{|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\) are less than \(\varepsilon\), so the supremum of that set, \(\omega_f(\eta)\), is at most \(\varepsilon\). question: In the lecture, the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is defined as the supremum of \(|f(x)-f(y)|\) for all \(x,y\) with \(|x-y|<\eta\). Explain why, for a continuous function on a closed and bounded interval, \(\omega_f(\eta)\to 0\) as \(\eta\to 0\), and how this fact is used to show that \(f\) is uniformly continuous.
answer: Because \(f\) is continuous on a closed and bounded interval, it is uniformly continuous. Thus for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). Taking \(\eta<\delta\) gives \(\omega_f(\eta)\le\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, \(\omega_f(\eta)\to 0\) as \(\eta\to 0\). This limit property is precisely the statement that the oscillation of \(f\) on arbitrarily small intervals can be made arbitrarily small, which is the definition of uniform continuity.

answer: The modulus of continuity bounds the oscillation of \(f\) on any subinterval of length less than \(\eta\). For a tagged partition with mesh \(\|\mathcal{P}\|<\eta\), the difference between the upper and lower Riemann sums is at most \(\omega_f(\eta)(b-a)\). As \(\eta\to 0\), \(\omega_f(\eta)\to 0\), so the upper and lower sums converge to the same limit. This shows that the Riemann sums converge to a single number, establishing the existence of the Riemann integral for continuous \(f\).

answer: All sequences of tagged partitions whose norms tend to zero produce Riemann sums that converge to the same limit, namely the Riemann integral \(\displaystyle \int_A^B f(x)\,dx\). As the norm shrinks, the rectangles become thinner and their total area approaches the true area under the graph of \(f\) on \([A,B]\). Thus the limit is independent of the particular sequence of partitions and is interpreted as the area under the graph of \(f\) between \(x=A\) and \(x=B\).

question: The lecture states that the Riemann integral is linear: \(\displaystyle \int_A^B (F+G)\,dx = \int_A^B F\,dx + \int_A^B G\,dx\). Using the definition via Riemann sums, show how the linearity of the integral follows from the linearity of the Riemann sum with respect to the function, and mention the role of the interval \([A,B]\) in this argument.
answer: For any tagged partition \(P\) of \([A,B]\) we have \(S(F+G,P)=S(F,P)+S(G,P)\) because the Riemann sum is defined as a finite sum of terms \(f(t_i)\Delta x_i\) and addition distributes over sums. Taking the limit as the norm of \(P\) goes to zero preserves this equality, yielding \(\int_A^B (F+G)\,dx = \int_A^B F\,dx + \int_A^B G\,dx\). The interval \([A,B]\) is the domain over which the sums are taken; it determines the set of subintervals \(\Delta x_i\) and thus the structure of the Riemann sums that converge to the integrals.

question: Consider a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\) and a tagged partition \(P\) with norm \(\|P\|=\delta\). If we refine \(P\) by adding a new tag inside each subinterval, producing a new partition \(P'\) with \(\|P'\|\le \delta/2\), how does the Riemann sum \(S(f,P')\) compare to \(S(f,P)\) in terms of approximation to the Riemann integral? Explain the reasoning using the norm and the graph of \(f\).
answer: When the partition is refined so that the new norm \(\|P'\|\) is at most half of the old norm \(\delta\), each subinterval of \(P'\) is no longer than \(\delta/2\). Because \(f\) is continuous on \([A,B]\), the variation of \(f\) over any subinterval of length at most \(\delta/2\) is smaller than over a subinterval of length \(\delta\). Consequently, the rectangles in the Riemann sum \(S(f,P')\) have heights that are closer to the true function values on their subintervals, and the total area of these rectangles is a better approximation to the area under the graph of \(f\). In other words, \(S(f,P')\) is closer to \(\displaystyle \int_A^B f(x)\,dx\) than \(S(f,P)\) is, because the finer partition reduces the error between the sum of rectangle areas and the actual area under the graph.

answer: Because continuity of \(F\) provides, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|F(x)-F(y)|<\varepsilon\). Taking a partition with norm \(\|P\|<\delta\) guarantees that on each subinterval the oscillation of \(F\) is less than \(\varepsilon\). Hence the difference between the upper and lower Riemann sums is bounded by \(\varepsilon(B-A)\), forcing all Riemann sums to converge to a single limit. Taking limits as \(\|P\|\to0\) gives \(\displaystyle \int_A^B (F+G)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} S(F+G,P_n) = \lim_{n\to\infty} S(F,P_n) + \lim_{n\to\infty} S(G,P_n) = \int_A^B F\,dx + \int_A^B G\,dx.\) This holds for continuous functions \(F\) and \(G\) on \([A,B]\), because continuity guarantees the existence of the integrals. question: If \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\), explain how the modulus of continuity argument guarantees that the Riemann integral exists for \(f\) and \(g\), and consequently for \(\alpha f+g\).
answer: For a continuous function \(h\) the modulus of continuity \(\omega_h(\eta)=\sup\{|h(x)-h(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\) satisfies \(\omega_h(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(\eta\) so that \(\omega_h(\eta)<\varepsilon/(b-a)\). Any partition with norm \(<\eta\) then has upper and lower sums differing by less than \(\varepsilon\), proving \(h\) is Riemann integrable. Since \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous, they are integrable, and the linear combination \(\alpha f+g\) is also continuous, so the same argument shows it is integrable.

answer: Because both sequences of partitions become arbitrarily fine, for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n\ge N\) the norm of \(P_n\) and \(Q_n\) is less than a chosen \(\eta\). By the definition of the Riemann integral, the difference between any two Riemann sums from partitions with norm \(<\eta\) is less than \(\varepsilon\). Hence the two sequences of Riemann sums converge to the same limit. This independence of the partition sequence justifies calling that common limit the Riemann integral of the function.

question: In the lecture, it was shown that the Riemann integral of a linear combination of continuous functions equals the linear combination of their integrals. Suppose \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Explain why the Riemann sum associated to \(\alpha f+g\) is equal to \(\alpha\) times the Riemann sum of \(f\) plus the Riemann sum of \(g\), and how taking limits yields the linearity of the integral.
answer: Because a Riemann sum is a finite sum of the form \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (\alpha f(x_k)+g(x_k))\,\Delta x_k\).  Distributing the sum gives \(\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(x_k)\,\Delta x_k + \sum_{k=1}^{n} g(x_k)\,\Delta x_k\), which is exactly \(\alpha\) times the Riemann sum of \(f\) plus the Riemann sum of \(g\).  Taking the limit as the mesh of the partition goes to zero, the first sum tends to \(\alpha\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) and the second to \(\int_a^b g(x)\,dx\).  Hence \(\int_a^b (\alpha f+g)(x)\,dx = \alpha\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b g(x)\,dx\).

question: The lecture mentions that the Riemann integral is a linear operator that maps continuous functions to real numbers. Using the definition of a linear operator, verify that the integral satisfies additivity and homogeneity for continuous functions on \([a,b]\).
answer:
A linear operator \(L\) satisfies \(L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)\) and \(L( eta u)= eta L(u)\) for all vectors \(u,v\) and scalars \( eta\).  Taking \(L\) to be the Riemann integral on \([a,b]\), we have for continuous \(f,g\):

1. Additivity: \(\int_a^b (f+g)(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b g(x)\,dx\).
2. Homogeneity: \(\int_a^b ( eta f)(x)\,dx =  eta \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) for any \( eta\in\mathbb{R}\).

These equalities follow directly from the linearity of Riemann sums and the limit process, confirming that the integral is indeed a linear operator.

question: According to the lecture, the Riemann integral satisfies a linearity property: for continuous functions \(f,g\) on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\int_a^b (\alpha f+g)\,dx = \alpha\int_a^b f\,dx + \int_a^b g\,dx\). Using this, explain why this linearity holds for the integral but does not generally hold for the derivative operator.
answer: The integral of a linear combination of functions is the sum of the integrals of each component weighted by the constants, because the Riemann sum of \(\alpha f+g\) splits into \(\alpha\) times the sum for \(f\) plus the sum for \(g\).
